en: Raging without restraint,
Giving Aktulpar a stroke,
As though his father Khan Manas's
Spirit stood watching,
The noble boy called out.
Eagerly toward Talas,
The boy, excited and unhesitating,
‘When death comes, I shall die,’ he said.
‘For my departed father Manas,
I shall go and recite the Quran,’ he said.
When the boy reached the gate,
With her ribs torn apart by grief,
Your dear mother Kanykey
Was waiting to meet him,
Tears pouring from her eyes.
As the excited boy went on,
His mother came into view.
Grasping the lead rope and sobbing,
Your mother let out a shriek.
She wished to keep the guest overnight;
Your mother wished to begin her tale.
Shrieking, weeping, sobbing,
From her dear blackcurrant eyes
Tears streamed a whip's length;
From her dear quail-like eyes,
Your mother's tears flowed in separate streams:
“Oh, my foal, listen!
My white palace is what I lament;
I shall tell much of my grief.
Hear of the pit dug for me,
My orphan who has sheltered me,
Hear of my boiling misery!
If you are a human being, my orphan,
Hear the suffering that comes from within me!
My wealth, not valued at a penny,
Let me tell from when I scattered it;
Fleeing Talas, wandering on foot,
My foal, let me tell from my flight!
Back then, when your valiant father died,
The countless riches left by the valiant one,
When the six scoundrels came straight in
And divided the treasure,
When they plundered your possessions,
When the six scoundrels wreaked utter havoc,
When they found a vile way to deal with me,
Dragging me like a kok-boru carcass,
When they slashed my breast open—
Will God take me if I lament?—
I had prayed for an only child like you.
The six scoundrels' slashing of my rump,
Will it ever leave my very bones?
My son, the horses on the foothills had mottled heads,
You, the orphan left behind, were young;
When my Magnanimous One, your father, died,
This head witnessed plunder in this way.
I suffered humiliation from the scoundrels,
I suffered blatant violence from the six scoundrels.
Abyke and Kobosh, two scoundrels,
From these I suffered beatings;
Chyybyt and Kochkor, four scoundrels,
From these I suffered plunder;
Adybay and Kolbay, six scoundrels,
I plainly suffered imprisonment.
The forty companions left by your father Manas
Drew their bows like rain;
From those I suffered humiliation.
My gold became like coal,
They ruined my treasure as they grew fat.
My silver was not like coal;
They grew fat, not knowing my burning pain.
The forty were khans from forty places,
They had settled in Talas.
Making coats no projectile could pierce,
I was your wretched mother.
Keep this in your thoughts;
Oh, orphan, never forget it.
When I lament, I have many words;
I tell my grief: listen.
Of Argyn and Kyrgyz mingled,
Let me tell the people's ways;
Of tamarisk-covered Keng-Kol and broad Talas,
Let me tell the nature of the land.
Hunched like a hunting hound,
Let me begin where I trotted along.
My foal, my son, listen;
Fleeing Talas, wandering on foot,
Let me begin where I came.
Grieving for my treasure,
Let me begin where I scattered it;
Carrying you away from Talas,
My son, let me begin where I fled.
I, your ill-fated mother,
Shall tell the nature of the people;
My orphan, if you take the road from here,
I shall tell the nature of the land:
If you leave Bukhara and travel,
If you travel far, not sparing your horse,
There is no mountain even an ankle-bone high,
There is no ravine even an ankle-bone deep,
There is no furrow touched by a plough,
There is no burrow dug by a marmot.
Looming mistily in corners,
Jutting into bays and angles,
The broad Ak-Chiy of broad Bukhara,
That is the place called broad Ak-Chiy.
Grieving and wandering to Bukhara,
I am the one who came in flight.
Without forgetting a hair's breadth of my words,
Keep them in your memory.
The great Ak-Chiy of broad Bukhara
You will cross in six days.
When you go beyond it,
Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoy—
You will reach Kul-Tokoy.
Let me tell of Kul-Tokoy:
Its birds hatched in the birches
Stand ready to fly;
Its birds hatched in the poplars,
My orphan, are eager to fly.
Its mountains have snow;
Its forest is full of rooks.
When its nightingale sings,
A sorrowful person could never leave.
When a parrot calls from a willow,
One in grief like me could not listen.
Apples ripen and turn to compost;
Walnuts fall and fill the ravines.
Its leaves are like hides;
Its black worms are thumb-sized.
It has small birds as large as snowcocks;
It has plane trees like towers.
It has separate patches of marsh,
It has geese flying in groups.
There are wild goats on its terraces,
Deer on its rough heights,
Argali on its foothills.
With ears pricked up,
No wolf has roamed there;
Trailing their tails,
No fox has roamed there.
There are plane trees as big as houses;
In the plane trees are these:
My son, look closely.
On one branch of the plane tree
A pied crow has hatched;
On one branch of the plane tree
A full-throated rook has hatched;
On one branch of the plane tree
An awkward-flying kite has hatched.
Look closely, orphan;
Every living creature has hatched there.
Removing the saddle, leaving his back bare,
Tethering Aktulpar by the leg,
Using the saddle as your pillow,
With your head toward the qibla,
Resting quietly upon your elbow,
Taking a little nap,
Sleeping your fill without haste,
Letting your winged steed graze,
That is a place to rest before going on.
When your mother fled in exhaustion,
Keeping alive for six days,
That is where your poor mother lay.
Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoy,
My sun, my orphan, do not forget it.
When you leave Kul-Tokoy,
When you pass onward,
There is pale-mottled, hazy Boz-Boltok.
You will reach Boz-Boltok;
When you climb Boz-Boltok,
May I take your misfortune upon me,
My foal, you will grow excited.
My orphan son, listen;
Your heart will be deeply troubled.
When you look ahead,
Renowned Kokand will appear.
My only orphan, listen:
If you enter Kokand, it will not treat you well;
Alas, orphan, it will not leave you unharmed.
Of Kokand below you,
The kushbegi in Kokand
Has little friendship with you.
If you enter Kokand, my orphan,
In the Kokand man's house
There is bozo set in a wooden vat,
Let him not seize and bind you,
My orphan who has sheltered me;
Let him not bring down a dark night,
Cut off your head and tie it on,
And go to the scoundrels Abyke and Kobosh
To announce glad tidings;
Let him not take the countless riches left by your father Manas
As his reward for the news!
The reason he would do so—
Your father used to inflict humiliation on Kokand;
From Alty-Shaar, Kokand,
Driving and beating them from there,
Six thousand silver ingots, a thousand otter pelts,
He used to take as tribute.
He used to imprison their dervishes;
When his anger was truly roused,
Your father used to beat their mullahs.
He used to seize and ruin their possessions;
Thus he used to wreak havoc.
That Kokand is no place to enter;
The kushbegi is no friend to you.
When you pass beyond it,
When you cross the gray saddle of land,
A pass with a green valley will come;
You will see a place like this.
That is the pass of Aman-Jol,
That is where your dear, disgraced mother came;
That is Aman-Jol itself.
There is no cawing crow,
No croaking raven in flight.
You will go on beyond that road,
My plump, gray-mottled goshawk,
My gray hawk, my morning star,
You whom I saw at death's door.
I have a night in which to see you once;
Whom have I besides you?
‘May my only child be safe,’ I prayed,
Crying out to the one God.
I tell of many kinds of road;
Listen carefully, my son.
You are a banner fastened to a spear,
You are a gift left by the Magnanimous.
My hoof left by the winged steed,
When you cross Aman-Bel,
When you pass beyond it,
You will come upon the Syr-Darya.
Looking, the eye could not encompass it;
Where it flowed could not be known.
I, your disgraced, wretched, deceitful mother,
My wealth not worth a penny,
When I scattered it in distraction,
Carrying you, my orphan,
I, your disgraced, ill-fated mother,
When I fled Talas on foot,
Grieving, weeping, coughing,
The old woman and the child,
This wretched soul bore with straining limbs.
Living through days of hardship,
I wandered away from Talas.
In winter's fiercest forty days,
I, your ill-fated mother,
That flowing Syr-Darya
Trudged across forty-two times.
I prayed for my only child.
The ice that formed in my marrow,
Even now, my only one,
Will it ever leave my very bones?
You will ford the Syr-Darya,
You will pass onward,
Chyyyrchyk and Salar, two rivers,
You will reach those two rivers.
